item.title: Caucus settlement
item.description:
Source: TW

Thread with excerpts from “The Archaeology of the Caucasus: From Earliest Settlements to the Iron Age” by Antonio Sagona.

Mountain passes in the Caucasus were glaciated in the last ice age - preventing anyone from crossing. Swidden (slash & burn) agriculture was common in Georgia & Armenia 4000-3000 BC, reducing tree cover & leaving much charcoal. In 3000 BC the fires abruptly ceased, the forests regrew, & plants associated with the steppe & pastoralism spread in the region.

item.title: Kin marriage prohibition
item.description:
Source: TW

Hindu Dharmaśāstras and Dharmasūtras prohibit sapiṇḍa and sagotra marriages, i.e. marriage with someone who is related within seven generations paternally or five generations maternally. In the modern Hindu Marriage Act of 1955 (which governs Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs in India), this prohibition has been relaxed to five generations paternally and three generations maternally, unless local custom allows it. The Kaḷaṣa likewise have a prohibition on intermarriage within seven generations paternally and four generations maternally. The former prohibition (prohibition on intermarriage within seven generations paternally) may plausibly be reconstructed for the Proto-Indo-Iranian culture as it is found even among the Nuristanis. There is no strong reason to assume that the Yaz Culture or Early Iranics were too different from their precursors.

item.title: wolf
item.description: The Arya really disliked wolves. Mostly because they used to eat our flock; our cows and sheep. This is why wolves are looked down upon in both the Rigveda and the Avesta. The vṛka/vehrka is a nasty animal. Thus the Arya pray to Viṣṇu & to Pūṣan to keep the wolf away. The word wolf itself is used in the RV to mean “hostility” in quite a few passages (i.e - क्व१॒॑ त्यानि॑ नौ स॒ख्या ब॑भूवुः॒ सचा॑वहे॒ यद॑वृ॒कं पु॒रा चि॑त्) where avṛka is “un-hostile”.
